question: How should massive (often MoE) LLMs be served across many GPUs and nodes: how to split prefill/decode, which parallelism to combine, how to accelerate decoding and route MoE tokens?
contributions: Disaggregated prefill/decode architecture, KV transfer with NIXL, Kubernetes/llm-d orchestration
Inference-focused TP/PP/EP/DP/CP strategies and hybrid combinations
Speculative decoding family (draft-target, EAGLE 1-3, self-speculative, Medusa), interleaved decode, constrained decoding
MoE dynamic routing: all-to-all optimisation, capacity factor, expert replication, adaptive routing

results.claim: DistServe, by disaggregating prefill and decode, served up to 7.4x more goodput requests within TTFT and TPOT constraints.
results.setup: DistServe system, as quoted by the chapter; model, hardware and workload not given
results.quote:
The DistServe system, by disaggregating prefill and decode, re-
ported up to 7.4× more goodput requests served within both TTFT and TPOT con-
straints (up to 12.6× tighter latency SLOs).

results.claim: DistServe also reported up to 12.6x tighter latency SLOs.
results.setup: Same as above
results.quote: (up to 12.6× tighter latency SLOs)

results.claim: Speculative decoding gives a theoretical k-times speedup but about 2x in practice.
results.setup: Generic two-model draft/target speculative decoding; no model or hardware
results.quote:
In practice, with overhead and occasional speculative-token rejections, the gain is
more like a 2× speedup.

results.claim: Empirical speedups of 1.5-2.5x are common for speculative decoding.
results.setup: Engines vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM; no workload given
results.quote:
Empirically, speedups around 1.5–
2.5× are common

results.claim: EAGLE reported up to about 3.5x speedup over vanilla decoding for a 4-token draft, preserving the output distribution.
results.setup: EAGLE paper numbers as quoted; 4-token draft; model not given
results.quote:
EAGLE reported up to about 3.5× speedup over vanilla decoding for a 4-token
draft while preserving the large model’s output distribution.

results.claim: EAGLE-2 is reported 20%-40% faster than EAGLE depending on task and model.
results.setup: EAGLE-2 paper numbers as quoted
results.quote:
EAGLE-2’s approach reported speedups of about 20%–40%
faster than EAGLE depending on the task and model.
results.note: Key Takeaways say 'EAGLE-2 reports up to 3.5× speedup (20%–40% more than EAGLE-1)', while the body gives 3.5x to EAGLE-1; the two attributions disagree.

results.claim: EAGLE-3 reports up to 6.5x speedup over non-optimized baseline variants and up to 1.4x over EAGLE-2.
results.setup: EAGLE-3 paper numbers as quoted; 'non-optimized baseline variants' undefined
results.quote:
EAGLE-3 reports
up to 1.4× improvements over EAGLE-2 in certain tasks—and up to 6.5× speedups
over non-optimized baseline variants.

results.claim: Medusa heads report about 2.2-3.6x speedups in published experiments, but about 2-3x in practice.
results.setup: Medusa-1 and Medusa-2 published experiments as quoted; requires retraining
results.quote:
Medusa’s multiheaded approach has reported about
2.2–3.6× speedups in published experiments across both Medusa-1 and Medusa-2.

results.claim: Self-speculative decoding (skipping every other layer for the draft) achieves a similar 2x speedup.
results.setup: Target model drafts using half its layers, possibly reduced precision
results.quote: achieves a similar 2× speedup as well.

results.claim: Consistency decoding (one LLM trained to generate and validate multiple tokens) produces about 3x speedup without a draft model.
results.setup: Chapter calls it 'consistent decoding'; no source named
results.quote:
This single-model approach produces ~3×
speedups without a separate draft model.

results.claim: Constrained decoding with compiled grammars can push overhead into the low single-digit percent range at scale for moderate constraints; complex grammars or small batches can still incur double-digit overhead.
results.setup: Simple JSON schemas, compiled grammars, mask computation overlapped with GPU execution
results.quote:
modern engines that use
compiled grammars and overlap mask computation with GPU execution can push
overhead into the low single-digit percent range at scale, but complex grammars
or small batches can still incur double-digit overhead.

results.claim: Recommended capacity factor is typically 1.2-1.5x the average token load; tokens beyond it go to a second-choice overflow expert or a second pass.
results.setup: MoE serving systems generally; no model or measurement
results.quote:
typically set at 1.2–1.5× the average token load, which caps how many
tokens each expert can process per batch. Tokens beyond that are routed to a sec-
ond-choice overflow expert—or queued for a second pass.

results.claim: Context parallelism cuts prompt-processing time roughly in half for every doubling of GPUs.
results.setup: Very long inputs, prefill only; no measurement given
results.quote:
This reduces prompt-processing time roughly in half for every
doubling of GPUs—with only a bit of overhead for cross-segment attention at the
boundaries.

results.claim: NVLink Switch Systems scale an NVLink fabric across up to 8 racks, 576 GPUs; TP is possible across it but intra-domain TP is recommended.
results.setup: GB200/GB300 NVL72 racks
results.quote:
NVLink Switch
Systems can scale an all-to-all, fully connected NVLink fabric across up to 8 racks,
or 576 GPUs (576 GPUs = 8 racks * 72 GPUs per rack).

results.claim: Worked 64-GPU hybrid layout: 60-layer, 64-expert MoE with 4-way PP (15 layers/stage), 2-way TP, EP over 16 experts per group with top-2 gating, two 64-GPU DP replicas.
results.setup: Illustrative cluster of 64 GPUs in 16 groups of 4
results.quote:
Using an
MoE with 60 layers and 64 experts, we can use 4-way pipeline parallelism with 15
layers per stage.

results.claim: Composition rule: TP up to diminishing returns (within a node or NVL72), PP minimally to fit, maximise EP, add DP replicas, optionally CP.
results.setup: Qualitative guidance for massive MoE serving
results.quote:
You would then
use pipeline parallelism minimally—just enough to fit the model in memory.
Then, you want to maximize EP to distribute MoE parameters across experts and
GPUs.

results.claim: Data parallelism for inference scales throughput linearly (ideal 10 req/s per GPU x 8 = 80 req/s) at 8x the memory and hardware cost.
results.setup: Idealised: independent requests, 1 GPU = 10 req/s, 8 replicas
results.quote:
using 8 GPUs
with 8 replicas ideally gives 80 requests per second of throughput

results.claim: A hot expert GPU at 99% utilisation while others average about 60% is the chapter's example of an MoE hotspot.
results.setup: Illustrative, not measured
results.quote:
utilization hitting 99%
while the other expert GPUs are averaging around 60% utilization

results.claim: In practice a capacity factor of 1.2 with top-2 gating is common.
results.setup: MoE inference; no measurement
results.quote:
In practice, a capacity factor of 1.2 (20% overflow allowance) with top-2 gating is
common.

results.claim: Constrained decoding costs a few milliseconds per token when backtracking is needed.
results.setup: Generic, no measurement
results.quote: often a few milliseconds per token

results.claim: Draft models should be typically 4x or more faster than the target for speculative decoding to pay off.
results.setup: Two-model speculative decoding
results.quote: typically by a factor of 4× or more

limits: No experiments of its own: every number is reported from other work or is an illustrative example, and most cited works (DistServe, EAGLE, Medusa, GLaM) are not given with references in the text.
Hardware focus is NVIDIA Blackwell (GB200/GB300 NVL72, ConnectX-8); advice is topology-dependent and the author says to profile.
Internal inconsistency: body says target verifies draft tokens 'one by one' while also saying it verifies the k-token sequence in a single batch (Fig 15-8 caption: multitoken verification).
Takeaways attribute 3.5x to EAGLE-2 while the body attributes 3.5x to EAGLE and +20-40% to EAGLE-2.
Capacity-factor advice reflects training-era MoE practice; chapter does not cover dropless routing or wide-EP.
Text contains typos ('float global collectives', 'FFP8', 'adaptive export routing', 'torch.nn.attendion').
practices: Disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools so TTFT and TPOT SLOs can both be met (Disaggregated Prefill and Decode; Key Takeaways).
Keep prefill and decode on compatible GPU families so KV layout and dtypes match (Disaggregated Prefill and Decode).
Place prefill/decode workers following the fabric: NVLink/NVSwitch in-node, GPUDirect RDMA across nodes; validate end-to-end KV transfer time (KV Cache Data Transfer and NIXL).
Deploy 1 NIC per GPU for PD disaggregation and MoE all-to-all (Impact on Latency).
Use TP within a single NVLink/NVSwitch domain; keep TP groups topology-aware even inside NVL72 (Tensor Parallelism; Hybrid Parallelism).
Use PP minimally, only to fit the model in memory (Hybrid Parallelism).
Use DP replicas for throughput, usually combined with TP/PP/EP (Data Parallelism).
Use CP only for very long contexts (100k+ tokens); for short prompts it adds outsized overhead (Context Parallelism).
Draft model must share the target's tokenizer and vocabulary (Two-Model Speculative Decoding).
Validate quality and speed before enabling layer-skipping or reduced-precision draft modes (Two-Model Speculative Decoding).
Always measure TTFT and tokens/s under your exact constrained-decoding schema; keep grammars compact (Constrained Decoding).
Use hierarchical two-stage all-to-all, double-buffering, chunked/pipelined exchanges and butterfly schedules for MoE (Expert Communication Optimization).
Collocate frequently co-activated experts, and compress activations to FP8/NVFP4 before all-to-all (Expert Communication Optimization).
Use capacity factor and replicate hot experts; alert when a single expert exceeds about 80% utilisation (Load Balancing; Adaptive Expert Routing).
Weigh complexity against ROI; start with the biggest bottleneck, prefill/decode interference (Key Takeaways).

terms.definition: A long prompt prefill occupies the GPU and delays time-sensitive decode work for other requests, and vice versa, when both are colocated.
Utilization and useful throughput at a given latency target.
terms.where: Scaling Prefill and Worker Nodes Independently

terms.definition: Assigning prefill and decode phases to different GPU pools so each scales independently.
NVIDIA library that moves KV cache, choosing NVLink/NVSwitch, RDMA or host-staged paths automatically.
terms.where: KV Cache Data Transfer and NIXL

terms.definition: Splits computations within each layer across GPUs with an all-reduce to aggregate partial outputs.
Partitions the model layer-wise across GPUs.
Distributes MoE experts across GPUs with all-to-all token exchange.
Partitions a single sequence of tokens across multiple GPUs, splitting the KV cache.
An overloaded expert stalls the pipeline because all expert computations must complete before progress.
Parameter capping tokens per expert per batch relative to average load; excess goes to an overflow expert or second pass.
A small draft model proposes k tokens that a larger target model validates in one batch.
The target model drafts with a fast approximate pass (e.g. half its layers) and verifies with a full pass.
Attaches multiple lightweight decoding heads to one LLM with tree-based attention to generate and verify several tokens per pass.
Restricting token selection so only valid tokens are allowed (JSON, grammar, banned sequences).
Placing frequently co-activated experts on the same GPU or node to avoid all-to-all hops.
Cloning a hot expert onto another GPU so the engine can split its load.
terms.where: Load Balancing, Capacity Factor, and Expert Replication
